utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we take the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Katarina Danicic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything that -- yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There is one matter I wanted to bring up with you before we started. I wasn't able to address it yesterday because we were running late. And if I could do it before the witness comes in; it may take me five minutes. And I guess I would like to go into private session because I make reference to a protected witness, and I have to discuss some names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was me who caused all this trouble, so I would like to apologise once again. It was really an honest mistake, because I just misspoke the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, before the witness is ushered in, I would like to correct the transcript of yesterday, and my friend from the Office of the Prosecutor brought my attention to it. It's page 13.772, line 2. I was quoting the document P405, and by quoting it I said -- I'm sure I said "SJB Doboj," but it was recorded as "CSB Doboj." So instead of "CSB," it should say "SJB Doboj," which is actually the quote from the document, and the document stays as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, good morning to you. Before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zecevic moves to wind up his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasic. I know that I kept you busy last night, but I hope that wasn't a big problem. Before we start dealing with that, I would like to return to something regarding which Mr. Olmsted intervened yesterday twice, and I somehow omitted his intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show 1D362.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you this is about criminal reports of the murder of one Muslim and one Croat in Doboj in August 1992. Mr. Olmsted's question was, or rather, his intervention, that these two criminal reports, which are both entered here, refer to the same event. So we -- we may have wrongly presented them as two events. So please take a look at the first document, 1D362, for which yesterday we established that it was not entered in the KU register.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it refers to four perpetrators of murder of one Ivan Cigoj and one Ferid Cabric, which happened on the 31st of July, 1992. One Vukojevic is mentioned as the first suspect, then Mirko Ninkovic, also known as doctor, then Jovica Vukojevic, born in 1973, and one Mladen; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please show the witness 1D355.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, 1D355, and there is a -- it is marked as entered in the crime register as entry 7/92, which must be on the first page, which we don't have, and this really is partly about the very same incident, but there's another perpetrator by the name of Zoran Ninkovic, aka Atata. The one in the previous document was Mirko Ninkovic, aka Doctor, and I established that the names of their fathers and mothers as well as their dates of birth differ. In this criminal report, we can see that this Zoran Ninkovic, apart from taking part in the breaking and entering and being an accomplice in the murder of those two men but also after the aforementioned four persons took those two men out of that flat and killed them, he stayed behind in the flat and committed -- or committed the murder of one Serb, one Milos Savic. Can you see that in this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me when I say that this -- these are actually two different incidents and two different cases, one against four persons and this one against Zoran Ninkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These incidents are partly linked. The public prosecutor's office could have merged them because they were committed at the same place, they started at the same place. However, this murder has been singled out. This Zoran Ninkovic, also known as Atata, had to be held responsible as a accomplice in the first murder of those two men. Possibly the public prosecutor's office asked the police to submit the reports under the same entry number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, in this case, apart from his being an accomplice in the murder of the two non-Serbs, he also committed another murder, and the other four were not suspects in this latter case.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we have clarified this, let us return to the documentation I handed you yesterday in the afternoon with the request to review it. It's about Sanski Most. In Sanski Most, if I remember your schematic correctly, you concluded that four crimes against non-Serbs were committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And six crimes where the victims were non-Serbs and the perpetrator is unidentified; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's was you established after reviewing the KU register of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I gave you a total of nine documents, tabs 4 through 12, from the Stanisic Defence documents list for you to establish whether or not each of these documents was entered in the KU register of Sanski Most, and if not, point out which weren't.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document that -- which you marked as number 4, concerning the murder committed by Nenad Malic against two victims, the criminal report was not entered in the police station because from the very outset of the investigation military security was involved. The police, as you can see from the documentation, assisted with the on-site investigation, and the criminal report was drafted by the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade so that from the very beginning through the end the investigation was conducted by military security bodies and then the police. This was only entered in the log-book of on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Document number 5 is similar. The suspects are Mile Gvozden and Miroslav. It's about the murder of nine Croats in a village. From the outset of the investigation, the services of military security were involved, and they also completed the investigation. The police only assisted with on-site investigations. That's why these two incidents were not registered, because the police didn't draft a criminal report nor was there a reason for them to do so. The decision of the first instance court of Sanski Most, that's document number 6, refers to KU 68/92 or is entered under this number. It's a decision in a trial for rape, as is mentioned in the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Case number 7 was registered as KU 93/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the crime of murder, and it can be found in the overview. So I said that these are already in the register. The murder of Petar Ivankovic and other persons, a total of four persons, was entered in the KU register in 1993. So it isn't included in this overview. The incident happened in 1992, but it was entered at the beginning of 1993. So this can be considered regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us the tab number of this document.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. On the yellow slip.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it's tab 8. If I understand you correctly, so the document under tab 8 was not included in your register because it was entered in the KU register in 1993, although the event itself happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a specific situation. A quadruple murder was reported, but the bodies were not found. It was later established that the bodies had been interred so that subsequently, pursuant to the orders of the public prosecutor's office and the court, some activities had been conducted, such as exhumation and autopsy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. Let's move on to tab 9.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This incident was entered as KU 75/92, and it's included in the overview and the summary. This involves four victims. The on-site investigation was conducted by the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tab 10?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, this is a letter written by Kajtaz and sent to one Vlado - I'm not sure Vlado who, but it must be a politician. It's some sort of a threatening letter. Unless he helps him concerning a criminal investigation, then he will say that this Vlado and some people in the power structure of Sanski Most ordered him to commit this murder. And it is entered in KU under 85/92. This is Ivo Tutic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And tab 12?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 12 refers to the same crime, but I must say that the offence under 75, with several victims: First, two persons were reported for whom it was established that they were present when the crime was committed, but later, in the investigation of the Military Prosecutor's Office which later on took over the case, it was established that the perpetrators were Kajtaz, probably the one who wrote this letter - and I say probably because I cannot be certain because I haven't seen the letter before - and one Maksimovic. So document number 12 is the indictment for the crime entered under KU 85/92. All crimes were entered except for the first two which were dealt with by the -- by military bodies, and there was no need for them to be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Some -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, document number 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I read the document number 11, and the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There's nothing in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There's nothing in the record, in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you and I also spoke about document under tab 11. It's a report about which you spoke about a murder refer -- on -- it's the same incident as the crime under tab 12.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document you marked under tab 11 refers to the same case that was entered under 85/92, KU 85/92. It's the murder of two persons, and the perpetrators are known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] So let's just conclude. These nine documents that I gave to you, two -- the first two documents relate to documents drafted by the military security; and for those reasons, because it was under the jurisdiction of the military justice system, they were not recorded in the Sanski Most KU, but they were probably registered in the record of investigations because the Sanski Most police assisted.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In tab 8, there is a criminal report submitted on the 25th of December, 1992, and it was recorded in the KU register only in 1993, although the event took place in 1992. And in that sense, your diagram should be augmented by that one incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to these two first documents referred to by the witness, drafted by the military security, these are tabs 4 and 5. For purposes of reference, these are documents 1D41 and P1282. Tab 8, the document that was entered into the register in 1993, this is document P116. I have now completed my cross-examination. Mr. Vasic, I would like to thank you, particularly for the assistance that you have provided on the clarification of facts regarding these documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasic. Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. Vasic, I'm Dragan Krgovic. I would like to introduce myself. I represent Mr. Zupljanin, and today I will be putting questions to you regarding your testimony to date and your statement provided to the Prosecutor. Mr. Vasic, in your statement and in your testimony, you mentioned -- actually, my question specifically relates to the Teslic register and specifically to one report, which is generally known to have been submitted and to have been acted upon. It was not actually entered or cannot be found in the register under the number that it bears. This is the report that was already talked about that refers to the Mice Group from Teslic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did check, together with the Prosecution, all the data on that criminal report, and I don't have the document in front of me now, but I think that it was registered under number 132 KU, but actually, it was actually not entered under that number but some other number. The only possibility why this could have happened was that the inspector who drafted the report in the Banja Luka CJB asked for the KU number by telephone, this was not entered immediately, and that is why this slip-up occurred. What's important is that the charge reached the prosecutor's office and that it was brought to trial. So in an analysis, these matters can perhaps cause some problems. These problems can occur when the CSB is in charge of the investigation and requests the KU number from the field, because the best practice would have been to go to the field, to record the report, and leave it there for operative records purposes, because in this case is this is not done what can happen is that we can look for a report, we don't find it because it's not entered anywhere, but it would have been submitted to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 2D27 now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the document. It has the registry office at the top, and then it has the number 132 KU, but that is not actually the official record number that it was entered under.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, can you look at page 2 of this document. The number of the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The perpetrators are listed starting from number 1 to number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the third page in the e-court now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sixteen perpetrators recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the statistics that you did for Teslic, when you spoke about the number of perpetrators and their ethnicity, that should also include - so that the data would be relevant and there would be a complete picture given of the work of the police in Teslic - this number should be included as well, these perpetrators who are mostly of Serb ethnicity; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been entered in the register. The register was analysed and perhaps this was not expressed, but now this document is known about, it belongs to Teslic, and is the result of the CSB centre in relation to breaking up that criminal group that had committed, as far as I know, several crimes in the Teslic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this page now where you can see the number -- or, rather, the charges. This is in the second paragraph. A number of crimes were committed, violating public law and order and traffic rules, participation in the group committing a crime. So, in essence, this would be a joint criminal enterprise, as crimes like this are now being treated in Bosnia, the group of persons who commit a number of crimes.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These persons are responsible for the disappearance of a large number of persons whose fate I think in that period was not resolved. They are responsible for taking them away and for their disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Also, illegal detention is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Illegal detention, taking them away, and their disappearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Murder, from Article 36.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And could you also look at page 5 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 5 in the e-court now, please, of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Using firearms, more than 30 people who were detained at the premises of the Teslic SB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what else is being referred to here are two more murders. And in item 5, also the killing of Hajrudin Becirevic and the killing of an army member who had taken part in their capture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in order to get the real picture about the work of the police of the Teslic municipality, regardless of the fact that this is not included in the register, it should have been included in your report. Over 30 killed, mostly Bosniaks and Croats, plus 16 of those charged and a large number of crimes involved. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I note -- I note for the record that his report does, in fact, address this particular case. So that is a slight misrepresentation. He mentions it in -- the substance of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the numbers were not included in the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You did not include these numbers in your report when you spoke about Teslic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I told you in the beginning that the report was based on the KU register. And this particular case, I mentioned that this was analysed with the Prosecution, the Prosecutor's office, and it was mentioned in the report. It was actually not in the register, and that's why it was not included in the statistical review.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The statistical review.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Had it been included in that review, the situation in Teslic would have been represented differently.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that means that at least 30 crimes with serious consequences had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which indicates that in order to give an assessment about the work of the police and the crimes, the KU, if it's the only source used, would be an unreliable means to show that?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the perspective of an analysis, you have data about crimes that are committed and then you can compare that to a previous period and compare to other agencies. This type of analysis is different. It was supposed to be done on the basis of the KU register. That's what was done. Perhaps if it had been compared to the diary and log-book of events and the log-book of investigations, perhaps the results would have been slightly different. But this is a relative matter. All we can speak about is what had been done to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What, actually, I would like you to confirm for me, in order to gain an actual picture - and I'm not talking about statistics because that can sometimes be the result of incorrect data - the result would have to include these types of criminal reports plus an analysis of the log-book of events as well as the log-book of investigations?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of crimes, investigations are much more important. This particular one is more important than 50 others because an organised group, practically a paramilitary formation, was broken up that had already established in specific territory its rule. Let me put it that way. And they worked upon the principle of they could do whatever they wanted. And that is why it's important that the police and the army recognise that at that point in time and they, let's say, eliminated this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, in replying to my question, you said that you made your analysis on the basis of the KU register. When you were doing your analysis, did you have the opportunity of looking at certain criminal charges? I'm speaking about Teslic now, specifically.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have the space or the time to go to Teslic and to deal with those matters. All I had were the KU registers in electronic form. I extracted the data from that. I didn't go any broader. I didn't even look at murders of non-Serbs by non-Serbs. I didn't deal with murders carried out by Serbs against Serbs. Only the questions as they were put in the table were dealt with for this particular statistical review.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When a crime appears in the register, the name of the perpetrator is recorded, the article he is being charged with, and if there are any victims, if that is known. Is that what is entered?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the perpetrator is unknown, that column remains blank until the person is discovered. The other columns can be filled in. In some places there are perhaps errors. And that means that sometimes the way the name of the victim is entered, we are not able to tell what their ethnicity is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And sometimes one person committed several crimes against a victim, and that is also something that you cannot see?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that you can see if the perpetrator is unknown, but if a person or a group is discovered and they committed a number of crimes, then sometimes this would be entered as sub-entries. And sometimes you would not enter all of the crimes involved, but you would just generally write the number of the crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you an exhibit, and that will be 1D03-1248.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if Mr. Krgovic could give a tab number, if it's from the Stanisic collection, that would be helpful, given the number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is number 28 in the Stanisic Defence binder. Can we have the B/C/S version on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just for the record, tab number 28 in the Stanisic Defence list is 1D03-12 -- 1284, and in the transcript it is said 1248. So it should be 1284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. You're completely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, take a look at this criminal report against these four persons. I believe that you dealt with it in your report. Do check, please.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, because this seems to be KU 249, but the total number of entries was 229, so I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's the very reason why I'm asking, because I believe that this is missing in the analysis, but I wasn't certain either.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This KU number, according to the documents I have at my disposal, wasn't used at all, so it couldn't have been included in my analysis. But this is about a group of four persons who committed a series of crimes. These are all unconnected crimes of robbery, but the public prosecutor's office and the court merged such offences because they were committed by the same group for -- in the extended period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the victims are Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they are all Muslims. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this log-book for Teslic does go to -- the one we have in our possession goes to entry 229. It's again possible, like the Doboj one we looked at yesterday, that there was a page missing. We can't know that again until we go down in the field and verify it. Because obviously if there's an entry 249, it seems like there's a page missing from this log-book. So what -- again, what I recommend we do is we send our investigator down, see if there's a missing page, if there is, photograph it, and we'll bring it back. And therefore the analysis is complete, because obviously this witness won't be coming back to testify as to the entry. But just to be understood that this witness, the log-book he had, the entry stopped at 229. That doesn't mean that there might have been another page missing. And so we'll look into that and report back to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, Mr. Vasic, the information from this report should have been included in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been entered in the KU register, they would have been, but if we can take a look at the last page of the Teslic register, then we'll see that the last entry is 229. We can take a look at the copy that we have and clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask my learned friend the Prosecutor to display the last page of the Teslic register.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can I have assistance from the Prosecutor? Can we have the last page of the log-book from Teslic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while we are waiting for this and to add to the confusion about the number of the document, I was told it was not you that was citing the wrong number but the number is wrong in the list of Stanisic Defence. It is 1D03-1248, as you said. So now I hope the transcript will be correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The Teslic Crime Register is 65 ter 10494.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So can we have this document on the screen. [Interpretation] Let us see the last page of this log-book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please let's see the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because then the document is entered. Yes. Here's a number 249, but is there the previous page too? These robberies are not included. Can we go back to the previous page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I am told that there is no previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen this page. That's why I'm saying that I need the previous one, because I would like to see the page where it says that the last entry is 229.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We've loaded the entire crime register for Teslic for 1992 that we have in our possession. It is in e-court. I think because it was loaded in a particular format the Registrar's having a legal bit of trouble going back to the previous pages, but they are there. What we could do is put them on -- well, if we had a moment, we can put it on Sanction and then we can, from here, flip back and forth between the pages. But, again, I represent that there could be a couple missing pages from this log-book and that would really be the answer to that issue, that if the pages between 229 -- covering entries between 299 and 249 are the ones that are missing, then that's just a matter of us going down, back to Teslic, checking the log-books, seeing whether those pages are simply missing or whether it was an error on our part in photographing them, and if it is the last -- or, well, actually, either way, we would notify the Trial Chamber as to the situation and the Trial Chamber could take that into consideration when they do their final analysis of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, I would like to ask the witness something to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you didn't include in your analysis entries from 229 through 250; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please enlarge this last page so we can see it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here we see 249.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three sub-entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, three sub-entries. And we may conclude that your analysis would have been complete for Teslic if you could have included the two missing pages.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The entries from 229 through 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No objection, with the proviso, of course, that once we figure out what the mistake is, or if there is a mistake, that we re-exhibit it with the full pages and in the proper order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps what we could do is we could mark it for identification now, and if the Registrar does not lock this document in the system, once we've sorted out this issue of the missing pages, we can reinsert them, we can put them in correctly, and then we can get it admitted into evidence at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I examined the witness based on the document as it is now, and he also made his analysis based on this document. So if the Prosecution wants to make a -- wants to make a bar table submission, then they may do so. But I just want to state for the record that the witness didn't have all relevant documents required for his analysis. But I seek to tender the entire document without the MFI marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it's the log-book you're -- you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But I will also tender the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue here is whether this particular case, which is under -- I guess -- is it -- I can't remember the KU number, but whether it is or is not in the log-book. And I think that's -- isn't that the issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The issue, whether or not it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Isn't the issue whether or not it is taken into account in the statistics this witness made?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that's -- that's true, but there's two issues there: One, did he miss it -- well, if it's -- one issue is whether the log-book represents it. In other words, is the log-book complete? It contains all the criminal reports filed by the Teslic SJB. And the way you can determine that is if you have the complete log-book with the missing pages and you can say, yes, this entry is in those missing pages and therefore the log-book was complete. As far as this witness is concerned, it's clear that he didn't consider it because he wasn't given those particular pages that are missing from this log-book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic's point is that we're dealing with what is today. The fact that there may be, upon further investigation, it may be discovered that what he in fact examined was incomplete is a matter still to be determined. The point is that today the witness's testimony and what he has done is based on what he had available. So we would admit it. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D97, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could the Registrar repeat, please, the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 65 ter number would be 10494.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 10494. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also seek to tender the previous document that I showed to the witness, 1D03-1248. It's a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we object to that because I think what this witness was able to say is that it is a crime that potentially involves non-Serbs and that if he had that page in the log-book he would have included it in his statistics. Beyond that, what's the need to admit it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours -- I apologise. This particular criminal report - you can take a look at entry 249 in the KU register - that is the very criminal report which was entered in the registry but was not included in the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you agree that what was entered under 249 was the criminal report that I showed you before?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a criminal report which has this entry number and the three sub-entries, 01, 02, 03.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That, too, is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D98, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness Exhibit 1D03-1316. I apologise. In the Stanisic Defence set, it's tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, take a look at this criminal report. Did you include it in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is KU 44/93. Although it refers to an incident from 1992, it was entered on 6 March 1993 in the KU register. My analysis did not include the following year because many acts committed in 1992 were only entered and dealt with in 1993, 4, 5, or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is about four persons?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four persons who committed a crime in the summer of 1992, but the criminal report was only filed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And we see from the narrative that there are several victims and that several crimes have been committed.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us turn to the following page. If you take a look at who the victims are, there are a number of names, but there are also Muslims: Hamed Hodzic, then Mehmed Rakic [phoen], Omer Rahic; then some Croatian family names such as Cosic, Baja Cosic and Ilija Cosic. And you would agree with me when I say that this is basically about crimes against Croats, Muslims, but also Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are some crimes in late 1992 and then early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in view of this principle providing statistics about the work of the police, these crimes should also be included, not on the basis of the analysis of the record but on the basis of a comprehensive analysis of the work of the police of Teslic in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. This is an indicator that regardless of when the crime was committed the police worked to -- to resolve those crimes. These crimes were committed in 1993 [as interpreted] and reported to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We were overlapping, and I am speaking quite fast. Your last answer was not translated. You, in essence, said these crimes were committed in 1992 and solved in 1993.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not all from 1992, as I have noticed. They were resolved in 1993, and that is when they were processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So a number of these crimes were committed in 1992 and some in 1993, but they were solved in 1993.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this document is from March 1993. It's outside the indictment period. We have no indication whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the witness has explained the relevance of that date, and we -- we had a similar document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that's fine, Your Honours, and I hope that when we present documents outside the indictment period that relate to events in 1992 that they also are admitted, similar case files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It depends, and we will see, Mr. Olmsted. This document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D99, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to look at two more criminal reports, but perhaps this would be a good time to go on a break, and then I will proceed to show these other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Before the witness comes in, or while he's coming in, I just wanted to raise a couple issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, could I deal with a matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- before you do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Prosecution filed a motion yesterday to amend the Rule 65 ter list -- ter exhibit list for Witness ST-197, who may be taking the stand in early September. And the Chamber would wish to inquire whether the Defence intends to respond; and if so, whether they can do so by Tuesday next, the 31st of August. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is with regard to what has just been admitted as 2D97, which is the Teslic SJB Crime Register. Having a look at it in e-court, I notice that there was only five pages, four or five pages, in e-court. I want to make it clear that that's not what this witness reviewed for purposes of this project. That's what he saw on the screen during his cross-examination. But what he, in fact, reviewed was a much larger range that covered the entire 1992 time period. And I just want to clarify that. I don't know if the Trial Chamber wants what he reviewed for purposes of this project or what he just saw on the screen, but just so the record reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the point was I showed that page to the witness, and the witness confirmed that that was not what he reviewed. This is what my request was, that the Prosecution did not show the witness this part that was not shown to him in the courtroom before. That was the point of showing it to the witness and tendering the document. That was the point of my cross-examination, that the complete documentation was not shown to the witness. And that's why I asked for that to be admitted. I had nothing against the Prosecutor showing in redirect that list and again dealing with that particular part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. That's -- but I just wanted to clarify the point that what -- that what he saw on the screen is not necessarily what he reviewed. He reviewed the whole log-book, and he was just shown one page, and that in e-court it's really just that one page that he was -- that's there. And if the entire log wants to come in, we can file a motion separately on that issue and deal with it there. But I just want the record to reflect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm thankful for your very last statement, Mr. Olmsted, because what I was about to say is that I have heard what each of you have said and I wasn't clear now as to what it was that the Defence was seeking to exhibit. So do I understand the position now to be that, for the sake of completeness, that really the entire log-book should be the exhibit and that the -- and then what -- the point that Mr. Krgovic has made about the part with which he specifically dealt with will fall into a context. Is that where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think we should have the log-book as it has been examined by the witness and as it is reflected in his statistics; that's it. And eventually, later, we can have the two or the three or the one page extra from entry 229 to entry 250 that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I think we're saying the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then ... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So I propose what we do is we correct what's in e-court. And we will download in e-court the entire log-book so it's complete. And then that would become that exhibit. And we'll notify the Registrar and the Court that we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that, of course, will include the page that Mr. Krgovic had before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is what I meant by the -- his point then having a context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The second issue is, I spoke to Mr. Krgovic and he believes that he might go into the third session today. I need -- currently I need about no more than a half an hour, I think, for re-examination. This witness is obviously a very high-level RS official, and I'm hoping that he can go home this weekend to attend to matters back in the Republika Srpska. Would it be possible, if Mr. Krgovic does go later than anticipated, that we go a little bit into the afternoon today just so that he may go home? From the internet site, it looked like there was courtrooms available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As usual, Mr. Olmsted, going beyond the fixed hours for the sessions requires extra services from the interpreters, from the audio video booth, and from the security officers, and everything else. So we're unable at this point to -- to see if we can accommodate your request, but the Registrar is just making the inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And in terms of making these arrangements, while you're on your feet Mr. Olmsted, it may be useful for you to say, so that the Registry can hear you, A, I assume you're talking about a half-hour break after we rise at 1.45; and B, how much extra time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll certainly know that once -- for certain after Mr. Krgovic is done with his cross-examination, but like I said, as of this point, I don't envision anything more than a half an hour. As far as any break, I don't need a break. But I will, of course, accommodate -- or we'd, of course, accommodate anything that's necessary for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, of course, the break is necessary both for the technical reasons, as we explain to each witness about the tapes, but also in terms of the interpreters and the convenience of everything. So the question of sitting beyond just running past 1.45 is really not practical. That is why I was asking you for your assistance so that the Registry knows what we're looking at. As -- as you now appreciate matters, if we did have to come back, what it would mean in terms of extra time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, again, I -- we wouldn't -- assuming that Mr. Krgovic does complete before the end of the third session, I wouldn't at this time need more than an additional session. It would certainly be significantly less than that. So we're looking at a fairly limited period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I will do my best to shorten my cross and just to show examples of documents. I'm not going to show all the documents that I planned. I will just show the witness one or two examples perhaps. I used this break for planning, and I think that I will manage to shorten my cross-examination and perhaps the third session will not even be required. I really will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. While the witness is on his way back to the stand, Mr. Zecevic, do I -- do we correctly infer that the exhumation issue is off the table for today and we're going to have to deal with that next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess so, Your Honours, because it is our -- it was our assumption, Ms. Korner's and mine joint assumption that it would take around two hours. So I'm not sure we will -- I'm positive we will have no time today, so we can start on Monday or whatever is the preference of the Trial Chamber. Maybe after we finish the next witness or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let us continue. I'm not that fond of statistics myself, but it seems that we need to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness, please, 1D03-1313. That would be tab 30 in the Stanisic collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this is a similar document as the one before. It's from an event from October 1992, setting of a facility on fire, and houses of ethnic Croats were set on fire. Since the perpetrator was discovered in 1994 [sic], this is in the register for 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. A correction to the transcript. The crime was committed in 1992 and discovered in 1993, not 1994. Mr. Vasic, precisely because of this entry it could not have been included in your statistical data for 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was not entered because the perpetrator was not found. It was -- it first had to be solved. It was solved in 1993 when the perpetrators were discovered. But the actual crime was committed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is part of that question that the Prosecutor put to you about whether this is possibly a war crime, arson?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are crimes of general endangerment, and they were not shown in 1992 but in 1993, and that is why they could not be included in the analysis of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And basically this is nothing unusual because sometimes much longer passes before certain crimes solved. It is a rare police in any country in the world who would immediately be able to find the perpetrator and process them.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what is important is a continuity, that crimes that were committed before should not be forgotten but should be worked on until they are resolved. So the police in this particular case managed to resolve of the matter in a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: According to the laws in effect in the former Yugoslavia, war crimes are never -- are never subject to the statute of limitations. Can you please just repeat this answer that you gave?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we now show the witness 1D03-1311. This would be tab 31 in the Stanisic Defence binder. Can we zoom in on the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, responding to a question by my learned friend Mr. Zecevic yesterday, you mentioned the submission of oral criminal reports. Mr. Zecevic showed you a certain number of such reports.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is one such report relating to Teslic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it says that this is a record of receipt of an oral criminal report filed by the plaintiff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And was this not processed in your report, or am I perhaps wrong?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29 December 1992. The register was closed on the 25th of December, so this was probably entered as item -- entry 66 in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The registers are closed five days or so before the end of the period to make possible a statistical analysis of crime trends and so on and so forth. That was the usual practice in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I repeat the same phrase: If we want to get insight into the overall crime situation in the municipality of Teslic, then we would need information about the events from 25 December till New Year's Day; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime was committed in 1992, and it would have to be included in the statistics for 1992, but the war crime trends don't change significantly if you close your register on the 25th of December, because the last five days of the current year will be taken into consideration in the following year. But talking about this particular crime, the victim was a Muslim and it was committed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just one moment. Mr. Witness, I see that this is about putting fire to four haystacks. Is that the kind of crime, perhaps because of the qualification as a crime of causing public danger, that would go into your statistics if it would have been in the KU log-book on an earlier date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The crime of causing public danger was considered in the -- the statistical analysis, so causing public danger by setting something on fire. But if public danger were to occur due to a spontaneous -- due to a spontaneous fire, it would not have been considered. But in this case, yes, this was considered in the statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please get an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would admit and have this document marked, Mr. Krgovic, but we -- we're curious as to how many other examples you're going to cite. You remember we would have walked this path yesterday with Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no more from the Teslic municipality. I wanted to show the witness some -- a dozen more documents or so, but I will refrain from doing that. I will move on. So this will be my last document from Teslic. I will continue showing the witness documents that have already been mentioned in the indictment in case they are not included in the statistics, but our -- but they -- but our clients are charged with them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit will be -- the exhibit number will be 2D101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, in your analysis in this annex but also in the previous analysis, you also included SJB Banja Luka, CSB Banja Luka, and Knezevo; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that in your statistical survey an important event is missing. I mean a criminal report about the Koricanske Stijene incident.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was talk about this case, and the issue was where that report was entered. It's actually the same as with the Mice in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness 2D39. I apologise. This is 2D35. Obviously my Case Manager made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us enlarge this a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here you see that the criminal report was filed on 8 September against an unidentified perpetrator. We see that the investigating judge headed the team that conducted the on-site investigation, and the criminal report was filed with some annexes, which means that criminal proceedings were launched; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter which is not marked KU. I don't know which KU could have been entered, perhaps the KU of the CSB or the KU register of Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But -- but you know that an investigation was conducted pursuant to this criminal report.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned about it in a later period because I was chief of the forensic centre, and the crime techs who went to the on-site investigation spoke to me about that, the problems they encountered, and the threats that had come from Prijedor concerning this matter. I believe that this Trial Chamber is familiar with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the officials who were processing this crime received threats from Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I would alert you that you have seven minutes of your one hour remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on the 23rd of August, I sent an e-mail requesting two and a half hours for this examination with regard to the documents that were received, that is, the witness's statement and the annexes. I will do my best to finish as early as possible, but I really can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So all this refers to the municipality of Knezevo, the event that happened there; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Knezevo borders on the municipality of Travnik, and I'm not sure whether that was a safe zone for conducting an on-site investigation because the separation line was near.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here we can see the list of annexes to this criminal report, that is, official notes of interviews and, what matters most to me, the list of people who were assumed to have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let us please show the witness 65 ter 1385. That is tab 24 of the Zupljanin Defence set.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that this is the list of persons who were assumed to have been killed at Koricanske Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To be used for identification, and it refers to the event near Skender Vakuf, a list of 44 persons on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that a total of 52 plus 80, that is 132, persons were identified as victims.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a total of 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only strange that the English version has 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm amazed too. And please read the remark at the bottom of the page. "The list is made according to the recollection of persons who survived the event near Skender Vakuf, namely those who were with them and taken off the buses."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I learned that some persons survived the incident. I believe that some returned to the territory controlled by the VRS, and they were placed in Banja Luka hospital, whereas some turned up in Travnik, and the media reported about it, so that it was public knowledge that they had survived, because they went over to the other side. But I didn't know of the crime at the time it was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see here under 49 a person from Kotor Varos by the name of Anto Draguljic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the Anto Draguljic whom I confused with that other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this incident, too, that is, this criminal report, and the number of victims, 80 in all, or 81 depending on which version you're relying on, if you -- if it had been entered in the crime register, it would have been taken into account in your statistical survey, and it would have changed the results substantially; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. But then all victims would have been included, because here the actual number of victims is probably much higher, twice as high as mentioned here, because the list is complete, but I wouldn't -- don't want to mention the precise number now because I would have to rely on my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But if you look at the criminal report, the initial assumption was that a total of 140 had been killed. That was mentioned in the criminal report. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the initial assumption, but the -- that changed. So if even five years later it was eventually established that they were 500 -- there were actually 500, then that would be the figure in our statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And proceedings are pending before BH courts for this crime; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that some persons have already been convicted, and proceedings are pending against a number of others. I believe that all perpetrators have been identified, and those who are alive are either being tried or their trial has already finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I have general question for you: You have discussed the topic with Mr. Zecevic and the Prosecutor already. When a crime or a potential crime and incident is reported and it is entered in the register and the police goes to the site and finds out that a crime has been committed and possibly identifies the perpetrator, if the police has the authority for investigation for this crime, then a criminal report is filed, it's entered into -- in the KU register, and this is considered in all registers and log-books; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If the police notes that, as it happened during the war, that the perpetrators are military personnel or it's a crime that is not automatically prosecuted, then the report is sent to the authorised military police or Military Prosecutor's Office, depending on the level of the work; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, the civilian police immediately gets in touch with the military police, and on that basis they agree on how to proceed. Most frequently, it was necessary for us to assist the military police because they had a shortage of crime technicians and equipment for them. So we always had to assist in the investigation on the scene and possibly regarding ballistics expertise and so on. Sometimes we also had to provide forensic experts to carry out the autopsies. So usually when a report was written we would monitor if they would take steps or not. If they did not take steps, then we would have to conduct the on-site investigation, and then later perhaps we would see who would actually be conducting the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, when a note from the investigation was sent, it did not go through the KU register but through the general log-book?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it went through the regular logs of the public security station. It was processed along with all the other general mail that was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. For example, there would be a shooting causing general danger; a person then, perhaps the police or the investigating judge, would go to the scene; information would be received that members of such and such a brigade, for example, in military uniform did the shooting; then the policemen on duty, whichever operative, would make an official note and send it to the military police or the military prosecutor. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The note would be sent later, but this would not be done so quickly on the scene without making sure perhaps that a representative of the military police was present, either from the prosecutor's office or the police, because they would have to be present during the investigative work. It would never be an urgent matter that the police then would deal with the on-site investigation and only later merely inform the military organs about the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Especially if the combat zone was close, and for certain reasons you couldn't wait for the military police?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would be many reasons why the military police couldn't come. Very often we would have to, without the presence of a prosecutor or investigative judge, carry out the on-site investigation, because they would inform us they couldn't be there. So we would have to do it without them. The same thing would apply for the military representatives. They would then authorise us to do the investigation without them. But the communication had to be quick enough so that immediately it would be quite clear under whose jurisdiction that particular matter fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So once the authority or jurisdiction of the military organs was established, a criminal report would not be submitted, and that event would not be entered into the KU register; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it would also happen that the police would submit a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator and then send that note to the military police for further processing?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the best way to go about it because then you would have the best overall picture of overall crimes. But as I said, the practice varied depending on the agreement between the prosecutor's offices and the military and the civilian police. Sometimes it would be entered into the register and most often it wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you something now. This is 1D352. And this is actually what caused all the confusion in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in on the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the criminal report yesterday for this Anto Draguljic, about his death.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at the paragraph -- one paragraph but last - if we can zoom in on there - where it says -- one paragraph but last where it states: "Considering that the area where the murder was committed was under the control of the army and in order to solve of this case we have also forwarded the official note to the command of the Light Infantry Brigade, the military police of Kotor Varos."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the usual procedure. Work was being done here as if the person entered some kind of military facility where the murder took place and the civilian organs were unable to conduct an investigation there. They couldn't conduct a comprehensive investigation. They sent the criminal report to the basic prosecutor's office, but this kind of property was immediately being sent to the Military Prosecutor's Office from there, and that was part of the co-operation among the prosecutors' offices. In the course of the investigation, they would be able to decide whether they would be in charge of a certain criminal prosecution, whether the civilian or the military prosecution would be dealing with that particular case. Incidents of a type where a person, especially at night when the visibility was low, would come to the guard post of a military post and would be killed was something that did happen during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this was nothing strange and unusual. The only thing was to investigate the matters and to show whether it was an accidental or whether it was a killing with a certain design or intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 of this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a note from the Infantry Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what is being asked is that since this was under the control of the army it should be the one to gather all the information regarding this particular crime.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now show the witness exhibit 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your answer was not recorded to my last question. The last question, this was when I asked you if the brigade was being asked to resolve this crime in view of the fact that this was -- let me put it that way, that this area was under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 10409, please. Can we look at page 113 in the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the record for Kotor Varos that you had the opportunity to look at, and now we will focus on this particular page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the third column from the top, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a record of all those cases that were in the course of being processed. This is not the official KU register. I have the wrong number, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which case are you seeking to deal with?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to show that that particular case was not recorded in the KU register. I think I've got the wrong number that I entered for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps I can resolve this confusion. The document you just showed involving the victim Anto Draguljic had a KU number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Murder 83 has been put in the KU register.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I just wanted to look at the notes on further work. I wanted to show that the note was not presented through the register. Otherwise, you would have noted that.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The criminal report was sent to the basic prosecutor's office -- all right. Oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, what is the purpose of pursuing this matter of Mr. Anto Draguljic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just asked the witness if these notes where the police, the military police, the military organs, were asked to work on a case were not processed through the register, and I wanted to show a specific example indicating this. This has to do with my previous question to the witness. I just wanted to confirm what the witness replied before to -- to this question. I wanted to show a specific example of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But I thought that it has long since been established that the log-books -- or the cases treated by the military police would be recorded in the military police's log-books and not in the civilian police's log-books. And I don't think that this is even a contested issue. I mean, it's clear that what the military police did was record it in their log-books, and what the civilian police did was, in turn, recorded in their log-books and their registers. So what is the purpose of repeating, once again, that there were a difference between the two sets of log-books, between the military and the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I actually wanted to finish with this question of yours because I think we did not clarify that with this particular witness regarding the records in terms of the military police. He was not asked about this. And that actually leads me to my next question that I wanted to put and which you have just pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I just may raise an issue because I think there is some confusion here and it's a little bit misleading. This particular case is in the SJB Kotor Varos Crime Register under KU entry 83/92. This witness has identified that entry in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but since the case was archived, which we can see from the register, we cannot see the work that followed on this case because a note was sent to the military police that they should continue to resolve this case. But then this could lead to the conclusion that nothing more was done regarding this case, and this is why I'm putting this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, he cannot put that question to this witness without putting on the screen entry 83/92 from the crime register so the witness can look at the column where it shows where the crime report was submitted to and confirm that there is no information as to where it was submitted to. But he -- without the register in front of him, he can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was looking for that document. This is actually the third entry from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what we have in front of us is the open cases log-book. It's not the crime register. We'll give you the ERN -- or the 65 ter number -- or P number for the crime register in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, perhaps this thing of mine, the witness can look at the second column and we can see that this case was archived. If we can look at the other page on the other side, the third entry from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a case number 83/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see "AA," that it was archived?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there is the KU number that is written there, too.
